title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
claim: Predicting latent tokens in both temporal directions with global and local targets yields contextual representations without collapse, usable bidirectionally at inference.
layout: 3 regions: legend and inset left, training center, inference right; bottom-to-top flow
description: A bottom-to-top pipeline diagram split into Training (center) and Inference (right) by a vertical gray divider. In training, a 3D human pose sequence of gray body renderings is divided into three chunks. An Encoder turns each chunk into a numbered latent token. Two weight-shared LatentFormers, drawn with small causal and reversed-causal mask grids, feed the tokens to Backward and Forward Predictors. The predictors output blue local components and green global components, and take an orange CLS token as input. The top-left inset shows the global/local decomposition. It uses a mean operation, subtraction nodes and orange double-headed arrows for the loss. A legend below it explains the token colors. In the inference panel, the LatentFormer has its masks crossed out in red, which shows unmasked bidirectional context.
caption: BAL learns movement representations from 3D pose sequences by bidirectional latent-space autoregressive prediction. The Encoder consolidates each chunk into a latent token, and a shared LatentFormer processes these tokens in both directions using causal and reversed causal masks. Two direction-specific predictors predict local components of adjacent latent tokens, while the global component is predicted from a learnable [CLS] token. At inference time, the LatentFormer extracts chunk representations without causal masking, enabling bidirectional contextual inference.
abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
